title: The Fever That Uncovered a Silent Hepatitis B Infection

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content: She is 45 years old. One week before this admission, she developed a continuous fever that didn't respond to medication. Two days before admission, she began vomiting — ten episodes, non-bilious, containing food particles — and roughly 10 hours before presenting, she had one episode of loose stools. She had typhoid fever a year earlier, but is not known to have tuberculosis, asthma, hypertension, epilepsy, or diabetes.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- General exam: conscious, coherent, cooperative
- Vitals: temperature 101°F, pulse 94 bpm, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, oxygen saturation 99%, capillary glucose 140 mg/dL
- Abdominal exam: obese abdomen, soft and non-tender, no bruits, no free fluid or palpable masses, no organomegaly
- Cardiorespiratory exam: unremarkable
- Neurological exam: normal
- Investigations sent: blood counts, biochemistry, ultrasound abdomen, and a fever work-up, which returned an incidental new finding of hepatitis B surface antigen positivity

Working diagnosis: acute gastroenteritis, with newly detected hepatitis B surface antigen positivity.

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
She was started on intravenous fluids, an anti-emetic (ondansetron), a proton pump inhibitor, and oral rehydration solution after each vomiting episode — standard supportive care for gastroenteritis, continued unchanged through day one.

By day two, with her fever and gastrointestinal symptoms not fully settling, her treatment was escalated to include intravenous ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, suggesting a bacterial component or additional infective process was suspected alongside her viral or infective gastroenteritis. This expanded antibiotic regimen continued through day three, run alongside the incidental hepatitis B finding that would need its own follow-up beyond this admission.
